title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close reading of Charles Dickens's last completed novel.
Our Mutual Friend is a book about money — about what it does to people, what it makes them pretend to be, and occasionally what it helps them escape.
It is also a book about dust heaps — vast, reeking mounds of Victorian London's waste — that happen to be worth a fortune.
And it is, underneath everything else, a book about resurrection — the recurring possibility that people and relationships can be remade.
To work through this extraordinary novel, I'm joined by three remarkable readers.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who has spent a lifetime reading novels as moral stories — stories about character under pressure, about goodness and its costs.
He is sceptical of politicised readings, and I suspect he will keep us honest.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows the institutions of Victorian England from the inside out — the workhouses, the courts, the dust economy.
When the novel touches the real world, James will tell us exactly how real it was.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has been re-reading it ever since.
She reads for the sentence, for the joke, for the moment that makes you put the book down and stare at the ceiling.
Let's begin with the world Dickens builds — the strange, class-scrambled, morally weighted atmosphere of Our Mutual Friend.
The atmosphere of this novel is established very early through a single, perfectly observed room.
When Silas Wegg first visits the Bower — the Boffins' home — Dickens gives us a space that is a compressed social history of sudden wealth.
The description is worth reading closely, because Dickens is doing something quite precise here.
"It was the queerest of rooms, fitted and furnished more like a luxurious amateur tap-room than anything else within the ken of Silas Wegg."
A tap-room — a public house saloon — that is luxurious.
That conjunction is the whole joke — and the whole tragedy — of the Boffins' position.
They have money enough for drawing-room furniture, but their instincts are still the settle and the sawdust.
And Dickens doesn't condemn them for it — which is the really interesting choice.
Precisely — and one notices that the carpet tells the whole story in miniature.
The flowery carpet advances so far and then — stops.
It gives way, as Dickens puts it, to a region of sand and sawdust.
"its glowing vegetation stopped short at Mrs Boffin's footstool, and gave place to a region of sand and sawdust."
That phrase — glowing vegetation — is doing remarkable work.
It is faintly absurd — carpet as jungle — and yet it conveys the Boffins' genuine aspiration with complete sympathy.
Dickens understood that character is revealed in the objects people surround themselves with — and that bad taste is not the same as bad character.
What I love about that room is the food.
On the fashionable side of the carpet, you have stuffed birds and waxen fruit under glass — hollow ornament, as Dickens calls it.
But on the sand-and-sawdust side, there is — and this detail is wonderful — the best part of a large pie and likewise of a cold joint.
"the best part of a large pie and likewise of a cold joint were plainly discernible among other solids."
Other solids — I adore that phrase.
The real nourishment is on the sawdust side.
Dickens is already telling us that the Boffins' instincts are better than their aspirations.
That contrast between real sustenance and mere display runs all the way through the novel's treatment of wealth.
Consider where the Boffins' fortune actually comes from — the dust heaps, the accumulated refuse of a city.
Dickens places enormous moral weight on who handles that inheritance honestly and who is corrupted by it.
And the novel's portrait of failed moral inheritance is perhaps most devastating in the Lammles.
There's a passage near the end of the novel — their final exit — that Dickens strips down to almost nothing.
"They walked arm-in-arm, showily enough, but without appearing to interchange a syllable."
Showily enough — that is the whole biography of a fraudulent marriage in two words.
And then Dickens delivers the sentence that I think is one of his finest endings for a character.
"In turning the street corner they might have turned out of this world, for anything Mr and Mrs Boffin ever saw of them to the contrary."
They vanish — not into death, not into ruin — simply out of the world's moral sight.
That sentence has the quality of a judgment delivered by the universe rather than the narrator.
Dickens doesn't need to say that they are damned.
He simply removes them from the ledger of human existence.
I think of Burke's phrase about the contract of the generations — the idea that the living, the dead, and the unborn are all party to civilisation.
The Lammles have broken that contract utterly — contributed nothing, taken what they could, and departed without leaving a trace.
The novel sets that emptiness against the Boffins' generous, slightly absurd, genuine warmth — and the contrast is withering.
But before we leave the question of women in this world — there's a passage I keep returning to, which offers something quite different from both the Bower and the Lammles.
Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren — the dolls' dressmaker — spend an evening together, and Dickens gives us a scene of such quiet intimacy that it almost stops the novel's momentum.
Lizzie brushes out Jenny's long fair hair, and this is what Dickens makes of that simple act.
"it fell in a beautiful shower over the poor shoulders that were much in need of such adorning rain."
Adorning rain.
It's tender, it's physical, it's unsentimental — those poor shoulders deserve the beauty that falls on them.
The friendship between Lizzie and Jenny is one of the truest things in the novel, and this passage is its emblem.
Money, dust, fraudulent appearances, and two women brushing each other's hair by firelight — we are, I think, already in the heart of this novel's world.
Coming up: we'll look more closely at the characters who move through that world — and what Dickens does with the question of who deserves to survive it.

segments.title: The Dust Heaps and the Social Scaffold

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — which is to say, with great pleasure and occasional outrage.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside the social machinery of the novel — the dust heaps, the money, the sycophants and the schemers who swarm around sudden wealth.
With me are three people who have thought hard about this book and are not shy about saying so.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose approach to fiction is unfashionably moral — and all the more useful for it.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what these institutions looked like from the inside — and from the court records.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic and reader who has lived with this novel since her teens and reads it aloud better than anyone I know.
We begin with the Boffins — and with what happens when the world discovers that a dustman has become very, very rich.
The passage that opens all of this — the Secretary reading the letters — is one of the great comic set-pieces in the novel.
Dickens is doing something wonderfully precise with scale.
Fifty-seven churches, forty-two parsonage houses, seven-and-twenty organs — the accumulation is almost musical.
And then, right in the middle of all that noise and piety, he drops this.
'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
Six words — and the Duke is already destroyed.
There's no verb, there's no subject even — just the letter, fat and self-important, announcing itself.
What strikes me is that the comedy never loses its moral precision.
The Duke's letter is 'lithographed by the hundred' — a form letter, personalised only in quite another hand.
The condescension is systematic, industrial, and entirely unconscious.
One thinks of Burke's observation that manners are of more importance than laws — and here the manners have entirely collapsed.
The postscript — 'The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas' — that is the masterstroke.
Dickens calls it 'thoughtful in the postscript,' which is about as withering a compliment as one can administer.
The institutional context here is entirely accurate, and that's part of what makes it sting.

Victorian charity dinners really did work this way — noblemen lending their names, stewards paying fees, the whole apparatus generating a thin slick of respectability over what was essentially a social transaction.
Boffin is being invited to buy his way into a class that will never fully admit him.
Three guineas at a time.
And then there are the individual beggars — which is, I think, an even finer piece of writing.
The taxonomy Dickens constructs is almost anthropological — the inspired beggar, the nobly independent beggar, the beggar of punctual business habits.
There's a whole society in those categories.
The line that stops me every time is about their documents.
'They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf.'
That image — minced veal to a calf — is grotesque and funny and faintly horrible all at once.
It captures something about how desperation produces its own degraded bureaucracy.
The word 'documents' is doing a great deal of work in that sentence.
These are people who have internalised the forms of legitimacy without any of the substance.
One might say the same of the Duke of Linseed, incidentally — the form without the feeling.
What Dickens is observing — with that novelist's cold eye — is that money, once rumoured, produces a kind of collective fiction.
Everyone who writes to Boffin has already written the story of themselves as deserving.
That instinct for self-narration is something you see constantly in the records of Victorian poor relief.
The distinction between the deserving and the undeserving poor was not just a moral category — it was an administrative one, and applicants knew it.
These letter-writers are trying to perform a narrative of worthiness — generals' daughters, devoted wives, divinely inspired unfortunates.
Dickens finds the comedy in the performance, but he doesn't quite let us forget the cold potato and the flickering lucifer-match behind it.
That tension — between comedy and genuine wretchedness — runs through the whole novel, doesn't it.
And it connects directly to the question of what money does to the people who inherit it — as well as to those who want it.
James, you've been looking at some of the novel's other characters caught in exactly that trap — people defined by their relationship to wealth they didn't earn and don't entirely want.
John Harmon is the most interesting case, I think, precisely because he is the heir who returns with something like self-suspicion.
He doesn't arrive in triumph.
Listen to how he describes it, speaking almost to himself.
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
Three times 'shrinking' and 'mistrustful' — the rhythm is almost penitential.
He fears that the money has already begun its work on him — that he is, as he puts it, 'already growing avaricious.'
Which is a remarkably honest thing for a man to say about himself.
That self-interrogation — 'Is that so? That is exactly so' — is one of those moments where the novel's moral seriousness breaks through the surface.
Harmon is conducting a kind of internal audit.
He is asking himself not merely what happened, but what it revealed about his character.
That is the question that animates the whole novel, in my view — not what the dust heaps signify, but what wealth does to the soul that receives it.
What moves me about that passage is the grief underneath it — the heartbroken sister, the sunlit childhood that wasn't.
He says his friends 'had made the only sunlight in my childish life' — and you feel the chill of the house he grew up in.
The money was never warmth. It was never home.
And yet here he is, pulled back to England by accounts of his 'fine inheritance' — the very thing he mistrusts.
There's a parallel figure worth considering here — Fledgeby, who represents a very different relationship to the social machinery.
Where Harmon is paralysed by self-doubt, Fledgeby is defined by a rather ugly self-knowledge.
He knows he didn't show to advantage, as he puts it — but he won't be managed on that account.
His challenge to Lammle is worth the words.
'Don't you on that account come talking to me as if I was your doll and puppet, because I am not.'
It's the grammar of someone who has thought carefully about exactly where the power lies, and is refusing to concede it.
Fledgeby is one of those characters Dickens gives almost no redeeming quality — and yet the portrait is not simply a caricature.
'The meanest of twinkles in his meanest of eyes' — the repetition of 'meanest' is precise in a way that a mere adjective wouldn't be.
He is mean in every sense — small-souled, calculating, ungracious.
But the refusal to be patronised — that is something.
Even the meanest characters in this novel insist upon themselves.
And then there is Wegg — who brings us back to the dust heaps themselves, and to one of the novel's stranger legal moments.
Wegg reads out the will he's discovered — very short, very cold — and what it says about old Harmon is almost more damning than anything said about the living characters.
He has left the Little Mound to Boffin and the rest to the Crown.

'Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.'
'Quite enough for him.' The contempt in that phrase is extraordinary — reaching out from beyond the grave.
And it goes to the Crown. To nobody. To the state as a kind of final snub to everyone who wanted it.
The legal detail is exact — a residuary bequest to the Crown was entirely possible and not unknown.
It tends to happen when someone dies intestate or with unrecognised heirs, but a deliberate choice to leave it there — that is another matter.
Old Harmon has used his will as a weapon — against his son, against any family, against posterity itself.
And yet his money still shapes every life in the novel.
The will, in this novel, is the ur-document — the ultimate piece of paper that defines everyone's station and everyone's story.
And Wegg reading it aloud to Venus, in his blandly buoyant way — there's a wickedness to that scene.
Wegg believes he has power, and power makes him expansive.
The novel is full of characters who mistake the possession of a document for the possession of truth.
Which brings us back rather neatly to Caroline's minced veal.
I am delighted to be brought back to the minced veal.
But Edmund is right — there's something systemic here about the fetish of documentation.
The beggars with their scraps, the Duke with his lithographed letter, Wegg with his discovered will — they all believe that the paper is the thing itself.
And Dickens keeps asking: but what is actually underneath?
That question — what lies beneath the paper, beneath the money, beneath the names people give themselves — seems to me the beating heart of this novel.
We'll carry it with us into the next part of our discussion.
My thanks to Edmund, James, and Caroline for a conversation that has been, I think, quite enough for all of us — in the very best sense.

segments.title: Bella's Vanity and the Question of Redemption

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's great preoccupations: what it means to change, genuinely change, and what stands in the way.
Bella Wilfer's arc from self-declared mercenary to a woman who chooses poverty for love's sake sits at the moral heart of the book.

But Dickens surrounds that arc with characters who are fixed, puppeted, crushed — Twemlow the human dining table, Sloppy in his catastrophic black suit, Bradley Headstone stalked by his own blind spots.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings his reading of character and moral imagination to all of it.
Professor James Blackstone will anchor us in the social and legal world the novel inhabits.
And Caroline Woodcourt, our close reader, will make sure we stop and savour the prose where it deserves it.
Sir Edmund, shall we begin with the novel's portrait of social performance — and perhaps with poor Twemlow?
Yes, and Twemlow is the perfect place to begin, because he is the novel's purest emblem of a man who has been entirely absorbed by the social machinery around him.
Dickens introduces him not as a person but as an object.
Listen to the precision of the metaphor — and to what it costs Twemlow personally.
"Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state."
The dining-table in its normal state — that is to say, empty.
Twemlow exists to be extended — and the more the Veneerings extend him, the further he finds himself from the centre.
That is not satire of a class system, precisely — it is a portrait of a man who has consented to his own erasure.
The moral question Dickens poses is always: what is a man willing to become?
What moves me about Twemlow — and I think it is genuinely moving beneath all the comedy — is that Dickens grants him dignity precisely by keeping the joke so absolutely deadpan.
He is stored over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street when not in use.
That detail is so exact and so pitiless that you almost wince.
But it connects to what Sir Edmund is saying about consent.
Twemlow has not resisted, and so the novel quietly stores him alongside the furniture.
Bella Wilfer, by contrast, is a character who starts in that furniture-like passivity and then refuses it.
The livery stable detail is historically precise, of course — that's exactly the kind of modest lodging a gentleman of reduced income but good connection would maintain in St James's.
But what Dickens captures is something the social historians call the tension between ascribed and achieved status.
Twemlow has ascribed status — the cousinship to Lord Snigsworth — but no achieved anything whatsoever.
He is borrowed, not respected.
And the Veneerings represent the opposite anxiety — they have money but no name, which in the mid-Victorian social calculus was almost worse.
Precisely — and it is worth noting that Dickens does not resolve the question of where dignity truly resides by being sentimental about poverty.
Look at what Mr Wilfer says when Bella comes to him having given up her wealthy prospects.
"I admire this mercenary young person distantly related to myself, more in this dress than if she had come to me in China silks, Cashmere shawls, and Golconda diamonds."
The joke — and it is a beautifully calibrated joke — is that Wilfer keeps calling her mercenary even as he celebrates her for renouncing mercenary values entirely.
Dickens is working through irony to arrive at genuine emotion — which is rather the method of the whole novel.
That speech of Wilfer's is one I have to read twice every time, because the syntax keeps wrong-footing you in the most deliberate way.
He builds that absurd formal distance — 'distantly related to myself' — and then breaks it open with 'I love this young person dearly.'
And the full weight of the passage lands here — listen to how he frames her choice as the truest fortune.
"She brings you a good fortune when she brings you the poverty she has accepted for your sake and the honest truth's."
Poverty and honest truth — that inversion of the conventional marriage-market language is breathtaking.
And it is worth being precise about what Bella is actually renouncing here, because the novel is.
The Boffin household offered her a trajectory into the propertied classes — real economic security in a world where women had almost no independent legal standing.
Dickens romanticises the choice somewhat — but he does not pretend poverty is comfortable.
He has given us enough of the Wilfer household — the cheerless dinners, the tyrannical Mrs Wilfer — to know exactly what Bella is walking back into.
Let's hold that thought about what people walk back into — because the novel also gives us characters who cannot escape what they are, however hard they try.
Sloppy is a comic instance of a body that defeats all attempts to contain it.
Sir Edmund, you've been looking at that passage — and I gather you find it doing more work than mere comedy.
The comedy is entirely genuine — one laughs, and one is entitled to laugh.
But Dickens's great gift is that the comedy never forecloses the humanity.
The passage describing Sloppy in his new black suit is one of the funniest in the book — and the key is that image of the buttons.
"He now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators."
A perfect Argus — the mythological giant of a hundred eyes, pressed into service to describe a boy whose suit will not lie flat.
The exuberance of the classical allusion is itself the joke — and the tenderness is in the word 'dazzled.'
The spectators are dazzled — not contemptuous.
The verbs are the thing — shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling.
Four of them, in that rhythm — it has the forward propulsion of a music-hall song.
And then Dickens piles on that extraordinary hatband — fluted behind, from crown to brim, terminated in a black bunch — 'from which the imagination shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted.'
The imagination shrunk discomfited — it is mock-heroic language deployed in complete earnest, and it is irresistible.
Sloppy's body is ungovernable — and in this novel, that marks him as someone the social system cannot quite absorb, which is almost a form of freedom.

That contrast with Twemlow is worth pressing on — Twemlow conforms so perfectly he becomes furniture; Sloppy cannot conform even when the tailor has received personal directions from Rokesmith himself.
The tailoring science fails — 'so much more powerful were the frailties of Sloppy's form than the strongest resources of tailoring science.'
The language of industrial progress — resources, science, cunning — is defeated by a boy's knees and elbows.
Dickens had a very clear eye for who the Victorian project of self-improvement was actually designed for — and Sloppy was not in the prospectus.
From a body that cannot be contained to a mind that cannot see its own danger — Bradley Headstone.
Sir Edmund, the passage you've been looking at here is one of the most chilling pieces of psychological writing in the book.
It is — and it requires no special pleading to call it psychological writing of the first order.
Bradley Headstone has committed murder and believes he has contained the danger — that he has managed Riderhood, has calculated every variable.
And Dickens gives us this — which I think is one of his most perfectly compressed observations.
"There are fifty doors by which discovery may enter. With infinite pains and cunning, he double locks and bars forty-nine of them, and cannot see the fiftieth standing wide open."
The arithmetic is everything — fifty doors, forty-nine locks, one standing open.
It is the logic of obsession precisely rendered: the very intensity of the effort creates the blindness.
And what haunts me is that word 'spell' — Dickens uses it twice in that passage.
Bradley is under a spell, and it is a spell that 'the shedder of blood for ever strives in vain' to break.
So we're in something almost mythological here — the same imaginative register as that Argus joke about Sloppy, but inverted entirely.
Sloppy's hundred gleaming eyes — and Bradley who cannot see the one door that matters.
The passage also does something very precise about Riderhood's role — and it connects to that earlier moment when Riderhood denounces Gaffer Hexam.

When Riderhood gives his information — 'The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed, his hand and no other' — he is performing certainty.
That solemn repetition — his hand and no other — is the language of a legal deposition, very deliberately so.
And Riderhood, who is himself a creature of the river's underworld, knows exactly how to put on that institutional voice.
Bradley thinks he has managed Riderhood — has fitted him into a safe place in the architecture of his guilt.
But a man who can denounce Gaffer with that cold formal fluency is not a man who can be managed.
Riderhood as the fiftieth door — standing wide open while Bradley bars all the others.
It is a magnificent irony.
And it places Bradley in the tradition of those literary figures — Macbeth is the obvious predecessor — who believe that will and calculation can outrun fate.
They cannot.
We have, in this one novel, a man who becomes a dining table, a boy whose suit defeats science, a woman who chooses honest poverty, and a murderer who cannot see the open door.

What unites them, I think — and perhaps our guests will push back on this — is the question of whether character can be shaped by will, or whether we are all, in the end, at the mercy of what we already are.
That is a question Our Mutual Friend refuses to answer simply — and it's one we'll carry into our next section.

segments.title: The Comedy of Secrets: Harmon's False Death and Narrative Misdirection

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're deep in what I want to call the comedy of secrets — the elaborate game of disguise and misdirection at the heart of this novel.
John Harmon is dead — except he isn't. He's the Secretary — except he's also Julius Handford. And somehow Dickens makes this gloriously, riotously funny.
With us, as ever, is Sir Edmund Leigh — our Oxford don who reads the novel as a story of individual character under moral pressure.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye — the institutions, the law, and what the real world of this novel actually looked like.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is our close reader — the one who catches the verbal music and the comic timing that makes these pages sing.
Let's begin with the question of identity itself — with that extraordinary moment when Harmon's multiple selves collapse into one.
The passage I keep returning to is the one where he strips away the disguise in a side street — sheds the oakum hair, the whisker — and simply becomes himself.
And Dickens describes what's revealed with this extraordinary formula, which he then doubles.
"became as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford, as never man was like another in this world"
That phrase — "as never man was like another in this world" — is doing something very peculiar.
It's the formula for saying two things are identical — and Dickens uses it for a man becoming himself.
And then the sentence does it again: John Rokesmith is equally, identically, the same lost Julius Handford.
Three names, one body, and the syntax performing the very confusion it's describing. It's a perfect trick.
What strikes me is that the comedy of disguise here is inseparable from something genuinely melancholy.
Harmon has chosen to efface himself — to be nobody, or three nobodies — because the inheritance that was supposed to liberate him arrived at the cost of everything he might have been.
Consider the Boffin passage — where we learn what that inheritance actually entailed in human terms.
"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet — and send it spinning across the yard."
That image — the bonnet spinning across the yard — is grotesque slapstick in the service of something quite dark.
Old Harmon's cruelty was not abstract. It was domestic, physical, absurd — and it shaped everything John Harmon became.
The disguise, then, is not merely a plot device. It is the residue of a damaged boyhood.
Edmund is right to anchor it there, in the cruelty of old Harmon — but I want to pause on the legal dimension that Dickens is also navigating.
A man believed dead has, in law, no claims — on property, on identity, on the social machinery that governs inheritance.
Harmon's disguise is not simply theatrical. It is legally precise — he cannot surface without triggering processes he cannot yet control.
And Boffin puts his finger on the absurdity of the whole situation with characteristic bluntness.
"when the old man does right the poor boy after all, the poor boy gets no good of it — he gets made away with, at the moment when he's lifting the cup and sarser to his lips."
The cup and saucer — that beautiful, modest image for everything Harmon was owed and never received.
Dickens understood that the law creates victims not only by its violence but by its timing.
And yet Dickens won't let it stay tragic. The same novel that gives us that damaged boy also gives us Silas Wegg — and there the comedy has no mercy at all.
There's a scene where Wegg and Venus discover a document suggesting hidden wealth — and the physical comedy of their reaction is extraordinary.
Wegg's wooden leg keeps rising with his excitement, he keeps elbowing Venus, until he topples sideways and squashes him against the settle.
"both remaining in a kind of pecuniary swoon."
A pecuniary swoon. Two words. Dickens does it in two words.
And the beauty is that their greed has rendered them physically helpless — the body enacting what the mind is doing.
The great comic villains are always punished through the logic of their own appetites — and Wegg is no exception.
His dismissal at the end is, I think, one of the most satisfying moments in the entire novel — and the most economical.
There is a warning before the end — from the Secretary, Harmon himself — delivered with magnificent brevity.
"Be careful what insolent liberties you take in that gentleman's presence, or I will throw you after it."
That is not a threat one forgets. And Dickens, being Dickens, makes good on it — not with the window, but with something better.
The scavenger's cart. Yes. There is a certain poetic rightness to it that no legal instrument could improve upon.
Wegg has spent the novel treating the dust mounds as a treasury — his private inheritance. And he ends in the muck.
The passage is wonderfully precise about Sloppy's technique — he swings Wegg up like a sack of flour or coals, and then —
"Mr S. found it impossible to resist the temptation of shooting Mr Silas Wegg into the cart's contents. A somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity, and with a prodigious splash."
A prodigious splash. The narrator can barely contain himself.
Justice here is not a courtroom process — it is a flying arc through the London air and a splash into refuse.
What ties all of this together, for me, is that Dickens uses comedy to deliver justice more efficiently than tragedy ever could.
Harmon survives his false death, reclaims his name, and the man who tried to profit from his erasure ends in a scavenger's cart.
The novel's misdirection — the oakum, the whiskers, the three names — was always in service of that restoration.
And I think that's what makes rereading it so pleasurable — you watch the machinery working, knowing where it leads.
Machinery is exactly the right word — and it's a machinery built to delight, and to sting.
Edmund, James, Caroline — thank you. That, I think, is the comedy of secrets: a dropped bonnet, a pecuniary swoon, and a prodigious splash.
In our next segment, we turn to the dust itself — what it means, what it costs, and what Dickens builds from it.

segments.title: Character Transformation and Dickens's Narrative Architecture

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart — and puts it back together with fresh eyes.
Today we're exploring one of the novel's most remarkable achievements: the way Dickens builds character transformation into the very architecture of his narrative.
From Gaffer Hexam counting his river-money, to John Harmon's calculated resurrection, to Bella Wilfer's long moral journey — this novel is obsessed with the question of what money does to people.
With me today are three readers who each bring something essential to these questions.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that the novel's moral imagination matters more than its social programme — and he reads every scene as a test of individual character.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what poverty, institutions, and the law actually looked like in the world Dickens was describing.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and brings the irreplaceable perspective of the passionate, close reader.
Edmund, let's begin at the very opening of the novel — with a scene that feels almost ritualistic in its strangeness.
It is a scene of almost ceremonial economy, and Dickens knows precisely what he is doing with it.
Gaffer Hexam has pulled something from the river — something we understand, without being told, to have been taken from a dead man.
And what does he do with the money?
He washes it in the same river that yielded it, then performs this extraordinary little rite.
'He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—"for luck," he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket.'
The triple repetition is Dickens at his most deliberately incantatory.
But notice: this is not greed rendered abstractly — it is greed rendered as superstition, as folk ritual, as something almost pitiable.
Dickens is already building the moral architecture of the whole novel in this one small gesture.
And the hoarseness — that one word, 'hoarsely' — does so much work.
It's not merely a voice quality — it's the sound of a man whose dealings with the dead have roughened something in him.
I always think of Lizzie sitting there watching him — Dickens doesn't tell us her expression, but we feel her watching.
She's his daughter, and this is what she has grown up with — this is her inheritance from a father shaped entirely by the river.
Which makes Gaffer's own death by the river, later, feel almost predestined.
Predestined is the right word, and Dickens gives it to us with brutal efficiency when the body is finally identified.
Riderhood, who has spent the night searching for the man he falsely accused, finds the recovered body — and his reaction is three words of astonishing compression.
'Gaffer's done me. It's Gaffer!'
He can only think of what Gaffer's death costs him — the revenge, the satisfaction, the social leverage he has lost.
There is no pity in Riderhood; there is only accounting.
And that is precisely the condition the novel is diagnosing — a world where every human relationship is ultimately denominated in self-interest.
I would put it slightly differently — though I take your point entirely, Blackstone.
Dickens is not diagnosing a systemic condition so much as charting the moral consequences of particular choices made by particular souls.
Gaffer's fate is not capitalism's fault — it is the fate of a man who has allowed the river and its dead to become his entire moral universe.
Now consider what that implies for Lizzie — who grew up watching her father perform that obscene little luck-ritual over drowned men's money.
When we hear Lizzie speak of another ruined child — the little creature in the passage about drink and degradation — the parallel becomes pointed.
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle—if she ever had one, Charley.'
That parenthetical — 'if she ever had one' — is the kind of blade Dickens conceals inside a sentence.
The doubt about the cradle is a doubt about whether childhood itself was ever available to this child.
And Lizzie is speaking from experience — she knows this territory from the inside.
What moves me every time I re-read that passage is the way she addresses Charley — her brother — as if quietly reminding him: this was also us.
Charley has escaped through education and resents every reminder of where he came from.
Lizzie has escaped through — what exactly? Through moral seriousness alone, which Dickens awards her almost as if it were a natural gift rather than an achievement.
But the compassion in that line is real and earned — she sees that other child and recognises something.
The detail about the father being 'a weak wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober — but a good workman too' is historically exact and almost unbearable.
That qualification — 'but a good workman too' — is precisely what Victorian charitable institutions couldn't process.
The deserving and undeserving poor were categories that required a binary verdict, and this man refuses the binary.
Which brings us, I think, to Boffin's magnificent tirade about charity titles — because this is Dickens attacking the institutions of benevolence from the other end.
The poor man who drinks and works is invisible to the charity machine; meanwhile it is busy generating titles for people who give five shillings.

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
The accumulation of those hyphenated titles is Dickens performing bureaucratic absurdity — turning it into a kind of savage comedy.
Rokesmith sitting 'up to his neck' in these documents is a perfect image of an honest man buried by institutional vanity.
Boffin is one of Dickens's great ventriloquist turns — he's supposed to be the Golden Dustman, simple and good-natured, and yet Dickens keeps giving him these devastating pieces of social analysis.
'If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain't he a Patron' — that 'ain't' does everything.
The grammatical roughness is deliberate — Boffin is not a gentleman, and his outrage is precisely the outrage of a man who hasn't learned to be polite about hypocrisy.
And it lands all the harder for that.
I want to resist the temptation to read this purely as social satire, however accurate the target.
Because what Dickens is tracing, across all these passages, is something more fundamental: the question of how a soul relates to money.
John Harmon lying in his bed in the public-house, recovering from near-death, is the moral centrepiece of this whole architecture.
He has escaped the fate his father's riches seemed to demand — and now he must decide what to do with that escape.

'The dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches—the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil—was strong upon the moral timidity that dates from my childhood with my poor sister.'
'Moral timidity' — that is not a phrase a satirist writes; that is a phrase a moralist writes, and it changes the register entirely.
Harmon is not simply outwitting the system — he is trying to purify his own conscience before he dares to love someone.
That is fair — and I'll grant you the phrase is remarkable.
But the scheme Harmon devises — to remain dead, to test Bella — depends on a very particular legal and social reality.
The will's power to bind two strangers in marriage is the hinge on which the whole plot turns — and that was entirely plausible Victorian legal territory.
The 'fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches' is not metaphor — it is the literal mechanism of testamentary tyranny.
Dickens understood, perhaps better than any other novelist, how the law of inheritance could function as a form of posthumous cruelty.
And Bella has to live inside that cruelty — she is the woman the dead man's will has assigned to a stranger she's never met.
Her transformation over the course of the novel is, I think, the most emotionally demanding thing Dickens asks us to follow.
She begins angry, mercenary, brittle — and those qualities are entirely understandable given her position.
What Dickens is building toward, very slowly, is the moment when she chooses to stop being that person — when the test Harmon has devised from his hospital bed actually works.
Whether we believe that transformation is a separate question — but the architecture holding it is extraordinary.
That word — architecture — keeps returning, and perhaps that's the right note on which to pause.
From Gaffer's ritual over the dead man's coins, to Harmon's calculated disappearance, to Boffin's furious inventory of phantom patrons — Dickens is building something vast.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the society that surrounds all of this — the Veneerings, the dinner-table world, and what Dickens makes of social performance at its most elaborate.

segments.title: Laughter and Critique: Humor as Social Commentary

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been moving through Dickens's great late novel with three extraordinary guides.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the moral imagination of a lifetime with the text.
Professor James Blackstone keeps us honest about the real institutions behind the fiction.
And Caroline Woodcourt reminds us what it actually feels like to read this book.
This segment is about laughter — specifically the kind of laughter Dickens uses as a scalpel.
Caroline, I want to start with you, because these comic scenes you've been looking at have a distinctly uncomfortable edge.
Yes, and I think that discomfort is precisely the point.
The Lammles are the place I keep coming back to, because the joke there is so perfectly Gothic.
There is a skeleton in the closet — not metaphorically, almost literally, in terms of narrative function.
And Dickens's narrator can't resist imagining the horror breaking through the performance.
He writes: 'How delightful those interchanges, and the looks accompanying them!'
'Now, if the skeleton up-stairs had taken that opportunity, for instance, of calling out Here I am, suffocating in the closet!'
That exclamation mark is doing enormous work.
It's the skeleton's voice — cheerful, impatient, desperate — and the narrator is ventriloquising it with obvious relish.
What strikes me there is the narrative's refusal to let social performance go unchallenged, even for a moment.
The Lammles have constructed a fiction of conjugal happiness from the very first morning of their marriage.
But Dickens will not let the reader simply enjoy the theatrical surface.
He insists on keeping the moral rot visible, and the Gothic intrusion of that imagined skeleton is how he does it.
It is a very precise form of satirical wit — the comedy is the accusation.
That passage also reminds me how thoroughly Dickens understood what fraud actually looks like from the inside.
The Lammles are not merely unhappy — they are practitioners of a sustained commercial deception towards their social circle.
And the novel is quite clear-eyed that their marriage is the institution that enables it.
But if you want to see fraud played for pure comic menace, Wegg is the character to examine.
His plan for extorting Boffin is rendered in this extraordinary mock-legal syntax — 'That, he would beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner.'
It reads like a bad solicitor's brief, and Dickens knows exactly why that parallel is funny.
Because blackmail and contract law were not always easy to tell apart in Victorian practice.
The word 'Halves!' is what I love most in that passage — the single word set off as though it were a legal verdict.
Dickens gives you the full oratorical buildup and then — that.
The passage reads: 'he considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, Halves!'
And then the scheme only escalates — Wegg floats Two-thirds, Three-fourths, always with that poisonous courtesy.
He ends by inviting his partner to correct him if he has been too generous — it's the satire of collaborative greed.
And then there's the phrase 'abject moral bondage and slavery' — Dickens makes Wegg use the language of abolition as a self-serving threat.
That is almost too much to absorb in a single reading.
Caroline is right that the language is doing something morally scandalous there.
Wegg co-opts the vocabulary of liberation in order to describe enslavement — and he does so without any apparent sense of the obscenity.
That unawareness is the mark of a certain kind of small villainy — the villain who has no tragic grandeur, only an appetite.
What Dickens understands — and this is where his moral imagination is at its sharpest — is that such people find their most natural expression in institutional language.
The bureaucratic cadence is the disguise.
Which brings us to the Deputy Lock scene, and that is a passage I find genuinely enraging, despite — or because of — how funny it is.
The Deputy pockets Betty Higden's coins one by one while simultaneously performing the rhetoric of honest toil.
The narrator describes how he drew his sleeve across his forehead, as if his petty corruption were the result of physical labour.
He says: 'I'm a man as earns his living by the sweat of his brow; and I won't stand in your way. Go where you like.'
The coins go into his pocket and the gesture of wiping the brow follows immediately — it is pantomime and it is perfectly observed.
But Betty Higden is fleeing the workhouse.
The comedy is purchased at her expense, and Dickens does not let you forget it.
And then there's the Wegg and the grindstone, which is a different register entirely — it's pure silent comedy, almost theatrical mime.
Wegg doesn't even speak — he just performs cruelty through gesture.
The sentence is so vivid and so strange:
'Silas made no reply, but laboured with a will at turning an imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it within; he then laughed silently, and stumped home.'
'Laughed silently' — that phrase haunts me.
It's not mirth, it's triumph — inward, private, unshared with us.
And 'stumped home' — that wooden leg rhythm — Dickens puts Wegg's whole character into a single verb.
There is something genuinely disturbing about that image — the imaginary grindstone is a power display with no audience but its victim.
And yet Dickens renders it as comedy, which forces the reader into an uncomfortable position.
Are we laughing with Wegg, or simply at the spectacle of a small man's cruelty?
I think the honest answer is: both, and Dickens intended exactly that unease.
What unites all of these comic moments — the Lammles, Wegg, the Deputy Lock — is that the joke always depends on institutional hypocrisy.
The performance of respectability, the language of contract and labour, the bureaucratic gesture — these are the masks Dickens keeps tearing off.
The laughter is the mechanism of exposure.
Laughter as exposure — that feels like a phrase worth sitting with before we move on.
There is something peculiarly Dickensian about making you laugh hardest at the moments of greatest injustice.
When we return, we'll be looking at the novel's darker currents — the river, the dust, and what Dickens makes of death itself.

segments.title: Closing: The Mutual Friend and the New Life

utterances.text: We come now to our closing segment — and what a novel to close on.
Our Mutual Friend ends not with a single resolution but with a whole constellation of them — some luminous, some devastating.
Edmund has been sitting with four passages that stretch from the Boffins' quiet contentment to Bradley Headstone's annihilation — quite a range.
Edmund, where do you want to begin?
With the simplest thing in the book, I think — and therefore, perhaps, the most profound.
We meet the Boffins early on, and Dickens gives us this exchange between husband and wife.
'Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!'
And then Dickens adds — with that perfectly placed satirical stab — that this warmth was, as he puts it, ruin to Mrs Boffin's aspirations.
They sit side by side, he tells us, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.
That capital U is doing extraordinary work — the whole comedy of social ambition punctured in a single adjective.
And yet the passage is tender, not mocking — that is Dickens's most difficult trick, and he brings it off beautifully.
That word — Unfashionable, capitalised — I've always loved it.
It's as if Dickens elevates their failure to meet society's standard into a kind of honour.
The Boffins are not good because they are wise or sophisticated — they are good because they simply cannot be otherwise.
And the novel knows that this kind of goodness is rarer — and more durable — than any fashionable virtue.
Which is exactly what the dead old miser perceived — and what makes his will so extraordinary a document.
Dickens takes us inside the mind of old John Harmon — this dead jailer, as he calls him — and what he gives us is almost a confession from beyond the grave.
The passage is worth attending to carefully.
'He had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt.'
Powerlessness — applied to wealth — is a word that would have startled Dickens's first readers.
And yet the logic is absolute: there are people who simply cannot be purchased.
The miser knows it — and hates them for it — and trusts them entirely.
That legal structure is worth pausing on, because it is genuinely remarkable.
Old Harmon is a man of absolute legal power over his household — and yet he inscribes that power's limits into his will.
He cannot compel the Boffins' loyalty in life, so he bequeaths them the means to exercise it after his death.
There is something almost — not quite, but almost — admirable in that final acknowledgement.
Dickens is careful to say the miser mistrusted all who bore any resemblance to himself — which is a devastating psychological aside.
And then, in the sharpest possible contrast, there is Bella.
The scene where Rokesmith rushes into the counting-house is one of the great comic-romantic moments in the whole novel.
Dickens piles on the breathless syntax — that triple repetition of 'not only' — until it becomes almost farcical.
And then he reads to us what Rokesmith cries out.
'My dear, dear girl; my gallant, generous, disinterested, courageous, noble girl!'
Six adjectives — six! — and the man is barely across the threshold.
But then Bella lifts her head and lays it on his breast — as if that were her head's chosen and lasting resting-place — and the comedy becomes something else entirely.
It becomes a kind of homing — a life finding its right place at last.
Bella's arc is, I think, the moral centre of the novel — more so, even, than the inheritance plot.
She begins as a creature of vanity — not a vicious vanity, but an unreflective one — and earns her way, through suffering, to genuine generosity.
Rokesmith's litany — gallant, generous, disinterested, courageous, noble — is not sentimental exaggeration.
By the time we reach that scene, she has earned each word.
Which makes Bradley Headstone's fate all the more harrowing by contrast.
Headstone is a man who has clawed his way up from the working poor through sheer will and discipline — and it destroys him.
The system rewarded him with respectability and gave him no instrument for managing what lay beneath it.
And then we get that passage — Bradley sitting through the night, Riderhood watching.
'Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard.'
The fire that should warm him instead ages him — it is consuming him from the inside.
That image of being overspread with ashes — it is not a metaphor Dickens reaches for carelessly.
The sentence does something extraordinary at the level of pure sound.
'The very texture and colour of his hair degenerating' — that word, degenerating, placed at the very end, falls like a closing door.
Bradley Headstone is not merely ruined — he is being unmade.
And what Dickens implies, I think, is that the self-made man carries within him the mechanism of his own unmaking.
It is one of the most morally serious passages in the book — all the more so for its silence.
Not one other word did Bradley utter all that night — Dickens tells us that, too.
The silence is its own kind of eloquence — a man who has lost all language for what he has become.
What strikes me, holding these four passages together, is how Dickens insists that character is destiny — but he means it in absolutely opposite ways for different people.
For the Boffins, their character is their salvation — their incorruptible simplicity protects them from everything the novel throws at them.
For Bella, character is something she must discover and then choose — and the choosing is the whole story.
For Bradley, character is the trap — the thing he built to survive that finally turns and devours him.
That is a beautiful way to hold the novel together — character as salvation, as discovery, as trap.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel that rewards patience — and re-reading — and the kind of sustained attention all three of you have brought to it today.
My thanks to Edmund Leigh, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation I shall be thinking about for a long time.
And thank you for listening to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

c5:p121.text:
It was the queerest of rooms, fitted and furnished more like a luxurious
      amateur tap-room than anything else within the ken of Silas Wegg. There
      were two wooden settles by the fire, one on either side of it, with a
      corresponding table before each. On one of these tables, the eight volumes
      were ranged flat, in a row, like a galvanic battery; on the other, certain
      squat case-bottles of inviting appearance seemed to stand on tiptoe to
      exchange glances with Mr Wegg over a front row of tumblers and a basin of
      white sugar. On the hob, a kettle steamed; on the hearth, a cat reposed.
      Facing the fire between the settles, a sofa, a footstool, and a little
      table, formed a centrepiece devoted to Mrs Boffin. They were garish in
      taste and colour, but were expensive articles of drawing-room furniture
      that had a very odd look beside the settles and the flaring gaslight
      pendent from the ceiling. There was a flowery carpet on the floor; but,
      instead of reaching to the fireside, its glowing vegetation stopped short
      at Mrs Boffin’s footstool, and gave place to a region of sand and sawdust.
      Mr Wegg also noticed, with admiring eyes, that, while the flowery land
      displayed such hollow ornamentation as stuffed birds and waxen fruits
      under glass-shades, there were, in the territory where vegetation ceased,
      compensatory shelves on which the best part of a large pie and likewise of
      a cold joint were plainly discernible among other solids. The room itself
      was large, though low; and the heavy frames of its old-fashioned windows,
      and the heavy beams in its crooked ceiling, seemed to indicate that it had
      once been a house of some mark standing alone in the country.
c5:p121.summary: Wegg observes the Bower's bizarrely hybrid interior: elegant drawing-room furniture mixed with tavern-style settles, books displayed like a battery, foodstuffs openly arranged, and a carpet that gives way to sand and sawdust, revealing the Boffins' uncertain class status and mixture of fashion and comfort.
c5:p121.best_quote: It was the queerest of rooms, fitted and furnished more like a luxurious amateur tap-room than anything else within the ken of Silas Wegg.

c52:p102.text:
She passed out and he followed her. Mr and Mrs Boffin had the curiosity
      softly to raise a window and look after them as they went down the long
      street. They walked arm-in-arm, showily enough, but without appearing to
      interchange a syllable. It might have been fanciful to suppose that under
      their outer bearing there was something of the shamed air of two cheats
      who were linked together by concealed handcuffs; but, not so, to suppose
      that they were haggardly weary of one another, of themselves, and of all
      this world. In turning the street corner they might have turned out of
      this world, for anything Mr and Mrs Boffin ever saw of them to the
      contrary; for, they set eyes on the Lammles never more.
c52:p102.summary: The Lammles depart arm-in-arm but in silence and spiritual wretchedness, walking with all the appearance of propriety but no genuine connection, and are never seen again—Dickens' final judgment on their morally empty lives.
c52:p102.best_quote: In turning the street corner they might have turned out of this world, for anything Mr and Mrs Boffin ever saw of them to the contrary

c28:p107.text:
It being Lizzie’s regular occupation when they were alone of an evening to
      brush out and smooth the long fair hair of the dolls’ dressmaker, she
      unfastened a ribbon that kept it back while the little creature was at her
      work, and it fell in a beautiful shower over the poor shoulders that were
      much in need of such adorning rain. ‘Not now, Lizzie, dear,’ said Jenny;
      ‘let us have a talk by the fire.’ With those words, she in her turn
      loosened her friend’s dark hair, and it dropped of its own weight over her
      bosom, in two rich masses. Pretending to compare the colours and admire
      the contrast, Jenny so managed a mere touch or two of her nimble hands, as
      that she herself laying a cheek on one of the dark folds, seemed blinded
      by her own clustering curls to all but the fire, while the fine handsome
      face and brow of Lizzie were revealed without obstruction in the sombre
      light.
c28:p107.summary: Lizzie offers to brush and smooth Miss Wren's long fair hair as they prepare for an evening talk by the fire, then Miss Wren loosens Lizzie's dark hair, creating a tender scene of mutual care and contrasting beauty.
c28:p107.best_quote: it fell in a beautiful shower over the poor shoulders that were much in need of such adorning rain.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

c30:p7.text:
‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.

On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.
